Not a fan of uv. Their complaints: it tries to do too many things; you still need `uv pip`, so it isn't a full pip replacement; it doesn't play well with Docker; and it adds complexity through new env vars like UV_TOOL_BIN_DIR, UV_SYSTEM_PYTHON and UV_LINK_MODE.

Moved off pyenv+poetry. Poetry versions had to be pinned because new releases stalled resolving dependencies, and pyenv needed the right system packages to compile Python on mixed macOS/Linux teams. uv is much faster, has a more ergonomic CLI, and solves both issues.
Objects to the recommended curl|sh and iwr|iex install methods. Beyond security, these installs tend to put files in random places, making them hard to manage and clean up.

For single-file scripts, adding a `#!/usr/bin/env -S uv run --script` shebang plus an inline `# /// script` block with requires-python and dependencies makes the script work like a standalone executable. uv installs and uses the listed modules automatically.
Prefers hatch from a FOSS perspective. Worries that adopting uv means more strings attached to a VC-funded company and reliance on its infrastructure.
Annoyance: uv doesn't seem to respect >= for a locally built wheel. With 6.4.1 published on GitLab and pyproject saying >=6.2.0, it still looks for the deleted 6.2.0 and errors out.

Plotly benchmarked uv to advise enterprise customers. They found almost all of the speed gain is lost if uv is configured to behave as much like pip as possible. The precompile flag alone can be ~50% of pip's install time for a typical data science venv.

Likes that uv mostly "just works." Dislikes that, like other package managers, it doesn't give a clear mental model of what's happening, so fixing the inevitable problems means diagnostic black boxes. Values time-to-fix over raw speed.

Several projects share a common wheel on an internal GitLab. They replaced about 10 lines of CI YAML with just "uv build" and "uv publish." Core dependencies are now visible instead of buried in a messy requirements.txt.
Puzzled that uvx (uv tool run) sometimes redownloads all dependencies it just fetched for another tool. "Downloading torch 15 times per day gets old even on 500 mbits."

Pet peeve: no elegant way to bump all dependencies to the latest versions their constraints allow. They wrote a script that parses pyproject.toml, removes the deps, and re-runs `uv add --upgrade`. Best features for them are uvx and PEP 723.
Complains there is still no option to store virtual envs outside projects after a year (GitHub issue #1495).

Once said they'd never use uv. On a shared server without root, with broken drivers, a 10GB quota, and pip's cache eating space while taking ages to install pytorch, they switched to uv and everything just worked. Now uses it for everything Python.
Won't migrate because uv, like many Python package managers, has no way to make --no-binary sticky. With pip-based tools like pipenv, they can at least use the PIP_NO_BINARY env var.
Coming from pip, uv is "confusingly fast." More than once they thought it hadn't worked because it returned so quickly.

Main gripe: uv is unforgiving with legacy setups, which quickly becomes a headache once you have ~4-5 in-house packages. Wishes minor version mismatches could be downgraded to warnings for progressive onboarding.
A big fan of uv, but has an 86GB dependency cache on their primary SSD, mostly from 50 different torch versions. Even uv can't salvage the mess of pip.

As a non-Python dev, finds uv makes Python much more accessible. You don't have to care about the many ways to create virtual environments; `uv run` handles the venv and Python install, "which is magic."
Some scientific packages are only available on conda, so lack of conda support means they must use micromamba instead of uv for some projects.

At launch, uv lacked a platform-agnostic lockfile, only producing platform-specific requirements.txt like pip-tools. Without that, this commenter called it dead-on-arrival as a "Cargo for Python." They praised --resolution=lowest and resolving against arbitrary target Python versions.
